newsitem.title: USA: Jones' lawyer outlines conditions for settlement.
newsitem.headline: Jones' lawyer outlines conditions for settlement.

text.p: A lawyer representing Paula Jones in her sexual harassment case against President Bill Clinton on Saturday set three conditions -- including a presidential apology -- for settling the case out of court.

Joseph Cammarata, one of two lawyers representing the former Arkansas state worker, said any settlement offer would need to include "some sort of an apology," an affirmation of the truthfulness of Jones' account of what happened between her and the president and a statement exonerating her of any wrongdoing.
"Those are some minimal requirements that if those are not presented, this thing is dead in the water," Cammarata told CNN's "Inside Politics Weekend."

He also said he and Jones' other lawyer, Gil Davis, would recommend rejecting any settlement offer that did not include some financial renumeration for "the three years of hell that Paula Jones has been put through, the humiliation, the embarrassment, having her name just dragged through the mud."
Jones won a victory this week when the Supreme Court unanimously rejected Clinton's appeal to have her suit delayed until after he leaves office.
She alleged that then-Arkansas Gov. Clinton made sexual advances to her in a Little Rock hotel in 1991, including exposing himself to her and asking her to perform oral sex.
Clinton denies the allegations. The Supreme Court made no ruling on the merits of her case, but said it should be allowed to proceed.

Clinton's private attorney Robert Bennett was not immediately available to comment on Cammarata's conditions, but on Friday he called Jones' allegations "malicious, baseless and politically inspired."
Bennett also ruled out any settlement that involved Clinton paying money to Jones or "acknowledging things that are simply not true."

Jones contends that she took the legal action to clear her name after American Spectator published an article claiming that Arkansas state policemen set up sexual liaisons for Clinton. One of the women in the article was identified by the name "Paula." Jones alleged this tied her to the case.
Cammarata declined to give more specific details of an acceptable settlement offer, saying it was up to the president's lawyers to make an offer if they felt it was appropriate.
He said Jones would donate any money received in the settlement to charity, after paying her legal fees and expenses. Jones had previously sought $700,000 damages.

The Supreme Court ruling sent the case back to a federal judge in Arkansas, where the lawsuit was filed in 1994, for more hearings. But it could be delayed by new motions by Clinton's lawyers seeking to dismiss the lawsuit.
